title: Module quiz: Async, concurrency and backpressure

blocks.text: Questions on what this page has just taught. Choose one answer for each.

questions.stem: Twelve tickets are sent together, and the provider refuses one with a 429. The team wants fewer refusals. What comes first?

options.text: Cap the parallel work with a semaphore, then pace what remains
options.says: The page's order is "Bound and pace first; retry last".

options.text: Raise the retry count so that each refusal is repeated sooner than before
options.says: Ruled out because "retrying a burst you could have avoided spends the time and the quota twice".

options.text: Send the work through more clients so that each one carries fewer calls
options.says: Ruled out because the page says "Don't create more than one client in the same application", since each has its own pools.

options.text: Raise the timeout on every request so that slow calls are not abandoned
options.says: Ruled out because the bound is what "protects the connection pool and the rate limit", and a timeout does not bound the burst.

questions.stem: A pipeline's first stage outpaces the stage behind it, and memory grows during long runs. Which fix is best?

options.text: Give the process more memory so that the buffer can hold the whole run
options.says: Ruled out because "the buffer is your memory".

options.text: Add a second producer so that the buffer fills twice as fast as before
options.says: Ruled out because "a fast producer and a slow consumer meet in an unbounded buffer".

options.text: Limit the buffer between the two so that a full one slows the producer
options.says: The page says "bound the queue between them: a full queue makes the model stage wait".

options.text: Retry the slow writes so that fewer of them fail during the long run
options.says: Ruled out because retries only repeat load, and "spends the time and the quota twice".

origin.section: Backpressure: the slow stage holds back the fast one

questions.stem: Each call takes two seconds, and the account may send ten requests a second. About how many calls run at once at that rate?

options.text: Five, found by dividing the latency by the throughput of the account
options.says: Ruled out because "requests in flight equal the rate times" the duration, with no division.

options.text: Twenty, found by multiplying throughput by latency
options.says: The page's relation is "requests in flight equal the rate times the call duration", so ten times two gives twenty.

options.text: Ten, the same as the sends that the account is allowed each second
options.says: Ruled out because the page says "Use the limit and your measured latency".

options.text: Two, the duration of a single call measured in whole seconds
options.says: Ruled out because "equal the rate times the call duration" keeps the rate in the product.

questions.stem: One ticket in a gathered batch fails with a bad request while the others succeed. What does the page's rule produce?

options.text: Only the successes, listed in the order in which they finished running
options.says: Ruled out because the pool "returns one outcome per item in input order".

options.text: Cancelled siblings and the first error raised to the caller of the batch
options.says: Ruled out because that is what a bare gather does, and "rejects on the first rejection" loses the rest.

options.text: A repeat of the failing item that continues until it finally succeeds
options.says: Ruled out because the pool "lets one failure stand alone" and does not loop on it.

options.text: An error record in its slot, with every other answer kept in order
options.says: The pool "returns one outcome per item in input order" and "lets one failure stand alone".

origin.section: The practice: a bounded worker pool
